extracted.intended_audience: newspaper editors, page designers, journalism students and general newspaper readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for newspaper page makeup and visual balance as shown on a historical New York Times page; aimed at informing page designers and journalists how to arrange cuts, headlines and boxes for balanced composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetrical balance in page layout
rubrics_metrics.description: In Plate III the position of the cut helped to effect symmetrical balance. Note the totally different effect achieved above through the placing of the two-column cut beneath a three-column head. Balance is preserved through the two single column boxes and the two-column headline at the left. Note how the position of the lower two-column heads helps to balance the three-column top head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place images (cuts), boxes and headlines so their sizes and positions counterbalance one another across the page. Examples: placing a two-column cut beneath a three-column head changes the overall effect; two single-column boxes plus a two-column headline at left can preserve balance; lower two-column heads can be positioned to offset a dominant three-column top head. Use positioning deliberately to achieve symmetrical (or intended asymmetrical) visual weight; consider relative column spans and vertical alignment when arranging elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial principle: 'All the News That's Fit to Print'
rubrics_metrics.description: ELEMENTS OF JOURNALISM — 'All the News That's Fit to Print.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement of editorial standard and newsworthiness: prioritize publishing material deemed appropriate and fit for the public. Serves as an overarching motto guiding selection and presentation of news items; implies judgment about relevance, propriety and public interest.
